To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the number of human neural stem cells transplanted into injured mouse spinal cord inversely correlates with the number of cells that survive and proliferate, and that the number of transplanted cells does not correlate with the number of human cells that migrate away from the transplant site.

the total number of human cells in the spinal cord after injury is not dependent on the number of cells transplanted, that the number of cells in the host spinal cord at 16 weeks after injury is inversely proportional to the number of cells that were transplanted, and that the number of human cells that proliferate in the spinal cord at two weeks after transplantation is inversely proportional the number of cells implanted.
the dose of human neural stem cells transplanted into spinal cord injured mice alters the dynamics of engraftment and proliferation of the donor cells.

the development of stem cell-based treatments for spinal cord injury.
the use of neural stem cell transplantation for the treatment of spinal cord injury.
the development of novel therapies for the treatment of neurological disease.

the transplantation dose alters the dynamics and the fate of hNSC after SCI.
